scope.title: Measuring amplitude and frequency with a CRO and Deriving and using the wave equation

owned_outcomes.outcome_text: understand the use of the time-base and y-gain of a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) to determine frequency and amplitude
derive, using the definitions of speed, frequency and wavelength, the wave equation v = f λ
recall and use v = f λ

scope.current_boundary: Consolidates legacy l03 and l04 into one unified lesson covering cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) trace measurements (y-gain, time-base, peak voltage, period, frequency), derivation of the wave equation v = f lambda from speed, frequency, and wavelength definitions, application of v = f lambda with prefix conversions, and direct synthesis of CRO frequency measurements with wave speed calculations. Internal CRO electron gun and deflection electronics, wave classifications (transverse/longitudinal), wave intensity, Doppler effects, and stationary waves are excluded.

9702_t07_cm01_l02: Wave definitions of displacement, amplitude, period, frequency, phase difference, wavelength, and T = 1/f.
9702_t01: Physical quantities, SI base units, prefixes (kilo, mega, giga, milli, micro, nano, pico), and uniform speed kinematics (v = d/t).

sources_inspected.demanded: Authoritative syllabus specifications: understanding use of time-base and y-gain to determine frequency and amplitude; deriving v = f lambda using definitions of speed, frequency, and wavelength; recalling and using v = f lambda.
Defines module cm02 lesson 3, binding outcome 9702_t07_m01_o03, skill 9702_skill_oscilloscope_traces, and key definitions and formulas.

Confirms consolidation: 9702_t07_cm02_l03 consolidates legacy l03 (CRO measurements) and l04 (wave equation derivation and use), owning outcomes 9702_t07_m01_o03, 9702_t07_m01_o04, and 9702_t07_m01_o05.
Confirms combined scope owning outcomes 9702_t07_m01_o03, o04, o05, skill 9702_skill_oscilloscope_traces, and primary evidence IDs.
Identifies question packages testing CRO graticule measurements, time-base calculations, wave equation derivations, and multi-step synthesis.

Supplies exact Cambridge definitions: period is 'the time taken for one complete oscillation or wave cycle'; frequency is 'the number of complete oscillations or wave cycles per unit time'; amplitude is 'the maximum displacement of a particle or point on a wave from its equilibrium position'; wavelength is 'the minimum distance between two adjacent points on a wave that are in phase'.
Supplies controlled LaTeX formulas: T = 1/f and v = f lambda.
Pedagogical flow for CRO measurements: screen as unlabelled grid, y-gain for vertical amplitude, time-base for horizontal period, multi-cycle spans, and scale comparison misconceptions.
Pedagogical flow for wave equation: one wavelength travelled in one period (v = lambda / T), substitution of T = 1/f to yield v = f lambda, symbolic rearrangement, and SI prefix compatibility.

Part (a)(i) requires calculating the time-base setting in s cm^-1 from known frequency (5000 Hz) and 1.5 cycles spanning 6.0 cm (or 1 cycle spanning 4.0 cm): T = 1/5000 = 2.0 x 10^-4 s, time-base = (2.0 x 10^-4) / 4.0 = 5.0 x 10^-5 s cm^-1.

Part (c) requires reading 1 cycle spanning 6.0 cm with time-base 5.0 x 10^-15 s cm^-1 to get period T = 3.0 x 10^-14 s, then calculating wavelength using lambda = cT = (3.0 x 10^8) x (3.0 x 10^-14) = 9.0 x 10^-6 m.
Part (a) requires determining period across 5.8 cm at time-base 5.0 x 10^-4 s cm^-1 (T = 2.9 x 10^-3 s), then calculating wavelength for sound at 330 m s^-1: lambda = vT = 330 x 2.9 x 10^-3 = 0.96 m.

Part (a)(i) demands symbolic expressions for distance moved by wavefront in time t (N lambda) and time t (N / f); part (a)(ii) deduces v = distance / time = N lambda / (N / f) = f lambda; part (b) determines frequency from CRO trace with time-base 0.20 ms cm^-1 (T = 4.0 x 0.20 = 0.80 ms, f = 1250 Hz = 1300 Hz).

Part (a) demands verbatim frequency definition; part (c)(i) requires reading period T = 4.0 cm x 0.50 ms cm^-1 = 2.0 ms to find frequency f = 1 / (2.0 x 10^-3) = 500 Hz from a trace that also displays y-axis setting 5.0 mV cm^-1.

Part (b)(i) calculates frequency from v = 330 m s^-1 and lambda = 0.18 m (f = v/lambda = 1800 Hz); part (b)(ii) calculates time-base setting from T = 1/1833 = 5.45 x 10^-4 s and 1 cycle spanning 4.0 cm on Fig. 4.1 (time-base = 1.4 x 10^-4 s cm^-1).

Assesses effect of adjusting time-base and y-gain controls: increasing time-base compresses trace horizontally (fits more cycles), while increasing y-gain compresses trace vertically (reduces trace height).

Assesses amplitude extraction from CRO: amplitude is measured from centre line to peak (2.0 cm), multiplied by y-gain (3.5 mV cm^-1) to yield 7.0 mV; highlights distractor using full peak-to-peak height (14 mV) or division.

concepts.name: Progressive wave definitions: displacement, amplitude, period, frequency, and wavelength
concepts.why_this_depth: Prerequisite foundation owned by Topic 7 CM01 L02 (outcome 9702_t07_m01_o02); provides the physical quantities extracted from waveforms.
misconceptions: Confusing amplitude with full peak-to-peak displacement.
Confusing wavelength (spatial distance between adjacent in-phase points) with period (temporal duration of one cycle).
demands: Recall that amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium.
Recall that period is the time taken for one complete cycle and wavelength is the minimum distance between adjacent in-phase points.

concepts.name: Period and frequency reciprocal relationship (T = 1/f)
concepts.why_this_depth: Prerequisite mathematical relationship owned by Topic 7 CM01 L02 and formula 9702_formula_period_frequency; links oscilloscope time measurements to frequency.
misconceptions: Forgetting to take the reciprocal when calculating frequency from period (reporting T directly as frequency).
Failing to convert time from milliseconds or microseconds into seconds before calculating frequency in hertz.
demands: Recall and apply T = 1/f and f = 1/T.
Convert period in seconds to frequency in hertz (s^-1).

concepts.name: Uniform wave speed definition as distance travelled per unit time (v = d / t)
concepts.why_this_depth: Prerequisite kinematics definition from Topic 1 (9702_t01); starting premise for deriving the wave equation.
misconceptions: Confusing the propagation speed of the wave pattern with the transverse or longitudinal speed of oscillating particles in the medium.
demands: Recall that speed is defined as distance travelled divided by time taken for uniform motion.

concepts.name: CRO screen graticule grid and dual-axis coordinate system: time-base and y-gain
concepts.why_this_depth: Foundational apparatus concept for owned outcome 9702_t07_m01_o03; establishes the screen as a two-dimensional calibrated measurement plane.
misconceptions: Assuming the axes of a CRO are permanently labelled in seconds and volts like standard graph paper.
Confusing which control scales the vertical axis versus the horizontal axis.
demands: Identify the CRO display as a graticule grid of major divisions (often 1.0 cm squares) and subdivisions (often 0.2 cm).
Identify that the vertical (y) axis displays potential difference / voltage scaled by the y-gain control.
Identify that the horizontal (x) axis displays elapsed time scaled by the time-base control.

concepts.name: Determining signal amplitude and peak voltage using y-gain
concepts.why_this_depth: Core skill of owned outcome 9702_t07_m01_o03; directly tested in Paper 1 and Paper 2 (e.g. 9702_s17_22_q05_c, 9702_s17_13_q23, 9702_s24_13_q22).
misconceptions: Measuring from the bottom trough to the top crest (peak-to-peak) instead of from the equilibrium centre line to a crest.
Dividing the vertical division count by the y-gain instead of multiplying.
Neglecting prefix factors such as mV div^-1 or microV div^-1.
demands: Locate the equilibrium or centre line of the displayed waveform.
Count the vertical divisions (or centimetres) from the centre line to a crest or trough.
Calculate signal amplitude (peak voltage V_0) using V_0 = (vertical divisions) x (y-gain setting).
Express amplitude with correct units (V, mV, microV) and appropriate significant figures.

concepts.name: Peak voltage versus peak-to-peak voltage distinction on a CRO display
concepts.why_this_depth: Clarifies the most frequent source of student marks loss on CRO amplitude questions; bridges practical signal measurement with definition 9702_def_amplitude.
misconceptions: Equating peak-to-peak voltage (V_p-p) directly with wave amplitude.
Failing to divide peak-to-peak height by 2 when determining amplitude from a signal without an explicit centre line.
demands: Distinguish between peak voltage V_0 (measured from centre line to crest) and peak-to-peak voltage V_p-p (measured from trough to crest).
Apply the relation V_0 = V_p-p / 2 when given peak-to-peak graticule measurements.

concepts.name: Determining period and frequency using time-base and multi-cycle measurement
concepts.why_this_depth: Carries owned outcome 9702_t07_m01_o03; tested extensively across Paper 2 (9702_m24_22_q05_c, 9702_m25_22_q05_a, 9702_s17_22_q05_c_i, 9702_s19_21_q05_b).
misconceptions: Measuring a half-cycle (e.g. crest to adjacent trough) and mistaking it for a full period.
Counting only the number of crests rather than the number of full wavelengths/cycles spanning a measured distance.
Failing to convert time-base units from ms div^-1 or micro-s div^-1 to seconds before calculating frequency.
demands: Identify corresponding points on adjacent cycles (e.g. crest to crest, trough to trough, or identical zero-crossings).
Count the horizontal divisions for N complete cycles to reduce measurement uncertainty.
Calculate period using T = (total horizontal divisions x time-base setting) / N.
Convert period T into seconds and calculate frequency using f = 1/T in hertz (Hz).

concepts.name: Determining time-base setting from known frequency or period and trace dimensions
concepts.why_this_depth: Inverted calculation pattern heavily tested in Cambridge Paper 2 (9702_m23_22_q05_a_i, 9702_m18_22_q04_b_ii).
misconceptions: Inverting the calculation by dividing divisions by time instead of time by divisions (e.g. reporting cm s^-1 instead of s cm^-1).
Using frequency directly in place of period without taking the reciprocal.
demands: Calculate period T from known frequency using T = 1/f.
Measure or identify the horizontal division count (or cm) for one cycle (or N cycles) on the graticule.
Determine the time-base setting using time-base = T / (divisions per cycle) in s div^-1 or s cm^-1.

concepts.name: Effect of adjusting time-base and y-gain controls on the displayed waveform
concepts.why_this_depth: Tested in conceptual Paper 1 and Paper 2 questions (e.g. 9702_s23_11_q20); critical for experimental competence and avoiding false inferences about physical wave parameters.
misconceptions: Believing that changing the time-base or y-gain knob physically alters the frequency or amplitude of the input sound or electrical signal.
Thinking that increasing the time-base (more seconds per division) stretches the wave horizontally, rather than compressing it to show more cycles.
Thinking that increasing the y-gain (more volts per division) makes the trace taller, rather than compressing it vertically.
demands: Predict that increasing time-base (s div^-1) compresses the trace horizontally, displaying more cycles across the screen.
Predict that decreasing time-base (s div^-1) stretches the trace horizontally, displaying fewer cycles.
Predict that increasing y-gain (V div^-1) compresses the trace vertically, decreasing its displayed height.
Predict that decreasing y-gain (V div^-1) stretches the trace vertically, increasing its displayed height.
State firmly that adjusting CRO controls alters only the visual scale of the display and has zero effect on the physical wave or input signal.

concepts.name: Deriving the wave equation v = f lambda from one period and one wavelength of pattern travel
concepts.why_this_depth: Carries owned outcome 9702_t07_m01_o04; mandatory syllabus derivation demand.
misconceptions: Claiming that a particle of the medium travels one wavelength in one period.
Writing down v = f lambda without demonstrating the intermediate steps linking distance, time, wavelength, and period.
demands: State that during one complete oscillation period T, the wave pattern or wavefront advances forward by a distance equal to one wavelength lambda.
Apply the definition of speed as distance divided by time: v = lambda / T.
Substitute the definition of frequency (T = 1/f or f = 1/T) into the speed expression: v = lambda / (1/f) = f lambda.
Emphasize that this derivation follows the advancing wave profile, not individual oscillating particles.

concepts.name: Deriving v = f lambda for an N-cycle wave train
concepts.why_this_depth: Explicitly assessed in Cambridge Paper 2 (9702_s19_21_q05_a_i and a_ii); tests general wave train logic.
misconceptions: Struggling to express total time t in terms of cycle count N and frequency f (writing t = N f instead of t = N / f).
Writing total distance as lambda / N instead of N lambda.
demands: State the total distance moved by a wavefront during N oscillations: distance = N lambda.
State the total time t taken for N oscillations: time t = N / f (or t = N T).
Deduce wave speed v = distance / time = (N lambda) / (N / f) = f lambda.

concepts.name: Recalling and applying the wave equation v = f lambda with prefix and unit conversions
concepts.why_this_depth: Carries owned outcome 9702_t07_m01_o05; tested in over 100 past paper questions.
misconceptions: Inserting numbers with mixed prefixes directly into the formula without converting to SI base units (e.g. multiplying kHz by cm directly).
Inverting algebraic rearrangements (e.g. writing lambda = v f or f = lambda / v instead of lambda = v / f and f = v / lambda).
Failing to recognize that all electromagnetic waves in free space travel at c = 3.00 x 10^8 m s^-1.
demands: Recall and state v = f lambda from memory.
Rearrange algebraically to solve for wavelength (lambda = v / f) and frequency (f = v / lambda).
Convert standard prefixes (kHz, MHz, GHz, mm, cm, micro-m, nm, pm) to SI units before numerical substitution.
Apply the speed of light c = 3.00 x 10^8 m s^-1 for electromagnetic wave calculations.

concepts.name: Synthesizing CRO measurements with the wave equation to determine wave speed or wavelength
concepts.why_this_depth: Key synthesis discriminant across Paper 2 (9702_m24_22_q05_c, 9702_m25_22_q05_a, 9702_m18_22_q04_b); unifies outcomes o03 and o05.
misconceptions: Treating horizontal divisions on a CRO screen as physical wavelength in metres.
Attempting to calculate wave speed directly from CRO trace dimensions without a known physical distance or speed in the medium.
demands: Extract period T and calculate frequency f from a CRO trace using time-base.
Combine the CRO-derived frequency with an independently measured physical wavelength to calculate wave speed: v = f lambda.
Combine the CRO-derived frequency (or period) with a known wave speed (e.g. speed of sound 330 m s^-1 or speed of light 3.00 x 10^8 m s^-1) to calculate physical wavelength: lambda = v / f = v T.
Explain why a CRO alone cannot measure physical wavelength without an external spatial scale or known wave speed.

concepts.name: Calibrated detent versus uncalibrated variable controls on an oscilloscope
concepts.why_this_depth: Practical experimental detail relevant to syllabus outcome 9702_t07_m01_o03 and Paper 3 / Paper 5 experimental methodology.
misconceptions: Assuming that graticule readings remain valid when the fine-adjustment variable vernier knob is rotated away from its calibrated position.
demands: Identify that quantitative measurement from a CRO graticule requires time-base and y-gain knobs to be clicked into their calibrated (CAL) positions.

concepts.name: Internal electronic architecture and electron beam physics of the cathode-ray tube
concepts.why_this_depth: Explicitly excluded by syllabus knowledge boundary: the CRO is used strictly as a measuring instrument.

concepts.why_this_depth: Belongs to course module 3, lesson 9702_t07_cm03_l05 (outcomes 9702_t07_m02_o01 and 9702_t07_m02_o02).

concepts.why_this_depth: Belongs to course module 5, lesson 9702_t07_cm05_l09 (outcomes 9702_t07_m03_o01 and 9702_t07_m03_o02).

hook.historical_investigation: Karl Ferdinand Braun (1850-1918) and the invention of the cathode-ray indicator tube in 1897 at the University of Strasbourg to visualize rapid alternating current waveforms.
hook.why_this_spine: In the late 1890s, the emergence of alternating current electrical power and high-frequency wireless oscillators created an urgent physical puzzle: alternating voltages reversed polarity hundreds or thousands of times every second, but mechanical galvanometers possessed too much physical mass and inertia to follow the rapid oscillations, showing only a stationary zero or a blurred vibration. Braun realized that cathode rays (beams of electrons) have negligible mass and inertia, allowing an electron beam to deflect instantaneously in response to alternating potential differences. By directing the deflected beam onto a phosphorescent screen and sweeping it horizontally at a known constant speed, Braun turned invisible, rapid electrical oscillations into visible, steady spatial waveforms on a calibrated grid. This historical breakthrough directly motivates the dual-axis operation of the cathode-ray oscilloscope.

verified_facts.fact: In 1897 at the University of Strasbourg, German physicist Karl Ferdinand Braun (1850-1918) constructed the first cathode-ray tube with a fluorescent screen, known as the Braun tube (Braunsche Rohre), to study variable electric currents.
verified_facts.source: Braun, F. (1897), 'Ueber ein Verfahren zur Demonstration und zum Studium des zeitlichen Verlaufes variabler Strome', Annalen der Physik und Chemie, Vol. 296, Issue 3, pp. 552-559.

verified_facts.fact: Braun investigated the severe limitation of mechanical galvanometers and moving-coil meters, which could not record alternating current waveforms because mechanical needles possessed too much inertia to respond to rapid oscillations above a few tens of hertz.
verified_facts.source: Nobel Lecture (1909), Karl Ferdinand Braun: 'Electrical Oscillations and Wireless Telegraphy', Nobel Media AB; Kurylo, F. & Susskind, C. (1981), Ferdinand Braun: A Life of the Nobel Prizewinner and Inventor of the Cathode-Ray Oscilloscope, MIT Press.

verified_facts.fact: Braun utilized a narrow beam of cathode rays inside a cold-cathode evacuated glass tube, recognizing that the particles forming the ray had negligible inertia compared to mechanical indicators and could deflect instantaneously under applied electromagnetic fields.
verified_facts.source: Braun, F. (1897), Annalen der Physik und Chemie, Vol. 296, pp. 552-559; Thomson, J. J. (1897), 'Cathode Rays', Philosophical Magazine, Vol. 44, pp. 293-316.

verified_facts.fact: To display the waveform against time, Braun initially reflected the phosphorescent spot in a rotating multifaceted mirror, which converted the vertical deflection into a continuous periodic curve of voltage against time.
verified_facts.source: Braun, F. (1897), Annalen der Physik und Chemie, Vol. 296, pp. 554-556; Susskind, C. (1968), 'Ferdinand Braun, Inventor of the Cathode-Ray Tube', Proceedings of the IEEE, Vol. 56, No. 9.

verified_facts.fact: Braun shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with Guglielmo Marconi for his foundational contributions to electrical oscillations and wireless telegraphy, where the cathode-ray tube served as the indispensable diagnostic instrument.
verified_facts.source: Nobel Media AB (1909), The Nobel Prize in Physics 1909: Presentation Speech and Award Ceremony.

hook.closing_question: How can a beam of electrons sweeping across a calibrated rectangular grid convert invisible, rapid vibrations of sound and electricity into precise quantitative measurements of amplitude, period, frequency, and wave speed?

visuals.purpose: Model multi-cycle measurement on a CRO trace to minimize fractional uncertainty in period determination, followed by the reciprocal conversion to frequency.
visuals.why_this_method: Detailed worked layout schematic showing a multi-cycle span bracket, division by cycle count, prefix conversion, and reciprocal step.
visuals.observed_features: A CRO trace displaying three full cycles across 12.0 horizontal divisions. A horizontal blue bracket spanning all three cycles is labelled 'Total span = 12.0 div; time-base = 25 micro-s div^-1'. An annotated flow shows: Step 1: Total time = 12.0 x 25 = 300 micro-s. Step 2: Period for one cycle T = 300 / 3 = 100 micro-s = 1.00 x 10^-4 s. Step 3: Frequency f = 1/T = 1 / (1.00 x 10^-4 s) = 1.00 x 10^4 Hz = 10.0 kHz. Annotation highlights: 'Measuring across multiple cycles spreads reading uncertainty across N repeats'.

visuals.purpose: Demonstrate the geometric derivation of the wave equation v = f lambda by showing a progressive wave advancing by one wavelength during one period of particle oscillation.
visuals.why_this_method: Two-frame motion diagram showing the wave profile at time t = 0 and time t = T, tracking the forward translation of a crest by distance lambda while a local particle oscillates through one cycle.
visuals.observed_features: Two vertically stacked panels of a progressive transverse wave. Upper panel at t = 0 shows a sinusoidal wave with crest 1 aligned with a vertical dotted marker. A particle on the medium at x = 0 is marked with an orange dot at equilibrium. Lower panel at t = T shows the wave profile shifted rightward so that the next crest has reached the dotted marker; a horizontal green dimension arrow indicates 'Distance travelled by wave pattern = lambda'. The orange medium particle has oscillated up, down, and returned to equilibrium (zero net travel). Accompanying derivation text displays: 'Speed v = distance / time = lambda / T; since T = 1/f, v = lambda / (1/f) = f lambda'.

visuals.purpose: Provide authentic examiner evidence of a microphone trace displaying multiple cycles used to determine frequency and derive wave properties.
visuals.why_this_method: Authentic Paper 2 examiner diagram from 9702_s19_21_q05 showing 2.5 cycles across 10.0 cm on a 1.0 cm graticule.
visuals.observed_features: Rectangular CRO graticule 10 major divisions wide by 4 major divisions high with 1.0 cm grid lines. Dimension markers at bottom right indicate 1.0 cm horizontal and 1.0 cm vertical. A horizontal centre line is located at y = 2.0 cm. A sinusoidal wave trace displays three identical crests at x = 1.0 cm, 5.0 cm, and 9.0 cm, each reaching y = 3.5 cm (amplitude 1.5 cm). Two complete cycles span 8.0 cm (4.0 cm per cycle). With time-base 0.20 ms cm^-1, T = 0.80 ms and f = 1250 Hz. Caption reads 'Fig. 5.1'.

activities.reasoning_step: Extracting the correct signal amplitude from a CRO trace by identifying the equilibrium centre line and multiplying vertical divisions by the y-gain setting, avoiding peak-to-peak confusion.
misconceptions_addressed: Measuring from the trough to the crest (full peak-to-peak height) instead of from the central equilibrium axis to a crest.
Dividing the graticule divisions by the y-gain instead of multiplying.
Neglecting millivolt or microvolt prefixes when converting to volts.

activities.reasoning_step: Determining period and frequency by evaluating multi-cycle horizontal graticule spans, converting sub-second units (ms, micro-s) to seconds, and applying the reciprocal relation f = 1/T.
misconceptions_addressed: Measuring a half-cycle (crest to trough) and mistaking it for a full cycle.
Counting crest peaks instead of intervals between identical phases.
Forgetting to invert period to find frequency (reporting period in seconds as frequency in hertz).

activities.reasoning_step: Inverting the CRO timing calculation to determine the required time-base setting given a known wave frequency and the graticule cycle width.
misconceptions_addressed: Dividing graticule divisions by period instead of dividing period by divisions (reporting cm s^-1 instead of s cm^-1).
Using frequency directly in place of period without computing T = 1/f.

activities.reasoning_step: Predicting the visual modifications to a displayed waveform when the time-base or y-gain knobs are altered, separating visual display scaling from physical wave properties.
misconceptions_addressed: Believing that changing oscilloscope controls changes the physical amplitude or frequency of the wave.
Confusing increasing the time-base (which compresses the trace horizontally) with stretching the trace.
Confusing increasing the y-gain (which compresses the trace vertically) with amplifying the signal.

activities.reasoning_step: Sequencing the formal physical derivation of the wave equation v = f lambda from speed, frequency, and wavelength definitions for both single-cycle and N-cycle cases.
misconceptions_addressed: Asserting that particles of the medium travel one wavelength in one period.
Inverting distance and time in kinematics formulas (writing v = t / d).
Writing total time as t = N f instead of t = N / f.

activities.reasoning_step: Selecting, rearranging, and computing wave parameters using v = f lambda with prefix conversions across sound, water, and electromagnetic waves.
misconceptions_addressed: Multiplying kilohertz or megahertz directly by centimetres or nanometres without converting to base SI units.
Inverting algebraic division when rearranging for frequency or wavelength (e.g. writing lambda = f / v).
Failing to use c = 3.00 x 10^8 m s^-1 for electromagnetic radiation.

activities.reasoning_step: Synthesizing a complete two-stage problem by reading period from a CRO trace, converting to frequency, and combining with wavelength or wave speed to determine the missing wave parameter.
misconceptions_addressed: Mistaking screen graticule distance on a CRO for spatial wavelength in metres.
Attempting to calculate wave speed solely from a CRO trace without external distance or velocity data.

unresolved.issue: Wave classification into transverse and longitudinal waves and particle motion analysis are deferred
unresolved.impact: Past paper questions (e.g. 9702_s17_22_q05_b, 9702_m24_22_q05_a, 9702_m16_22_q04_a) combine CRO frequency extraction with longitudinal or transverse particle motion questions.
unresolved.resolution: Declared strictly out of scope: this lesson teaches oscilloscope measurement algorithms and the wave equation, while transverse versus longitudinal wave comparison is owned by 9702_t07_cm03_l05.

unresolved.issue: Wave intensity relationships (intensity proportional to amplitude squared) are deferred
unresolved.impact: Past paper questions (e.g. 9702_m23_22_q05_a_ii, 9702_m18_22_q04_b_iii) ask students to sketch modified CRO traces when sound intensity changes (e.g. intensity increases to 3I so amplitude becomes sqrt(3) times original).
unresolved.resolution: Declared strictly out of scope: intensity = power / area and intensity proportional to amplitude squared are owned by 9702_t07_cm04_l07. Trace changes in this lesson are restricted to direct amplitude changes and CRO control adjustments.

unresolved.issue: Internal electronics of the cathode-ray tube are excluded by syllabus
unresolved.impact: Learners may wonder how deflection plates and electron beams work physically.
unresolved.resolution: The knowledge boundary explicitly states that the CRO is used strictly as a measuring instrument; electron gun and deflection physics are outside AS scope.
